entry.title: What is DLL hooking
entry.content:
Many EDRs hook commonly used or otherwise important APIs to monitor behavior, such as reading files, writing to memory, and creating processes. Whenever these APIs are called, the EDR becomes aware of them and checks whether the behavior is suspicious.

How to hook

Inline unhook

Directly modify the contents of the target API in a DLL.

  • Add a JMP/CALL instruction at the beginning of the DLL function to jump to the EDR.
  • The execution flow is therefore: call critical API → DLL API jump → EDR function → jump back to DLL API
    • It first goes to the EDR to perform the monitoring and logging it needs to do, then returns to the original API to complete its intended operation.

This usually happens when a process is created: the EDR injects its own DLL into the process memory and modifies the memory contents of the target DLL.

  • It locates the memory address of the target API and overwrites its beginning with something like a JMP.

How does the EDR know when a process is created? There are several methods:

  • Windows Native API

    • https://learn.microsoft.com/zh-tw/windows-hardware/drivers/ddi/ntddk/nf-ntddk-pssetcreateprocessnotifyroutineex
    • Such as PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEX, WMI, or user notification hooks

  • AppInit_DLL

    • https://learn.microsoft.com/zh-tw/windows/win32/dlls/secure-boot-and-appinit-dlls

    Allows you to load a custom DLL into the address space of every interactive application, making it easy to intercept system APIs.

  • Kernel driver

    • Intercept or modify APIs at the driver layer, such as ZwCreateProcess, or use ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) for real-time tracing. It can also inject its own DLL/agent directly during the process creation stage.

  • Remote injection mechanism (Remote DLL Injection)

    • Use APIs such as CreateRemoteThread, NtWriteVirtualMemory, and NtCreateThreadEx to inject the EDR’s monitoring DLL into the target process.
    • C/C++ APIs can be used to copy the DLL path into the other process’s memory and create a thread to execute it.

  • Automatically traverse existing running processes

IAT/EAT Hook

  • IAT Hook (Import Address Table): Modify the pointers in the import table so that an API that originally pointed to A.dll points to EDR.dll instead.
  • EAT Hook (Export Address Table): Modify the pointers in the export table to alter the DLL export function.

This does not modify the DLL itself; instead, it modifies the table pointers. A more advanced approach is to hook the kernel layer or syscalls, but that is outside the scope of DLLs here.

What is kernel32.dll

It is a commonly used DLL in Windows that provides basic system functionality for user applications and calls some lower-level APIs.

kernel32.dll is primarily responsible for basic operating system functions, such as file, memory, process, thread, time, and DLL management. It is one of the most important foundations for interaction between applications and the operating system kernel on Windows.

Many operations go through ntdll.dll before interacting further with the kernel.

Common API examples

  • File management:
    • CreateFileW / ReadFile / WriteFile / DeleteFileW
  • Memory management:
    • VirtualAlloc / VirtualFree / VirtualProtect
  • Process and thread control:
    • CreateProcessW / ExitProcess / CreateThread / TerminateThread
  • System time/timing:
    • GetSystemTime / Sleep
  • DLL loading/management:
    • LoadLibraryW / FreeLibrary / GetProcAddress

Execution Flow

Therefore, my understanding is that a program operates as follows:

It can be understood that almost all Windows applications automatically load kernel32.dll when they start. Therefore, hooking ntdll.dll or kernel32.dll makes it possible to intercept most behaviors that have a significant impact on the system.

Solve DLL hook

There are several approaches. Common ones include:

  1. DLL unhook: Restore the DLL and remove the hook.
  2. Direct syscall: Bypass DLLs that may be hooked and call the syscall directly.
  3. Indirect syscall: Use a legitimate DLL execution path to call the target syscall.

Unhook

Simply put, this involves finding the location of the hook. In the case of an inline hook, this means finding the jump at the beginning that redirects execution to the EDR to determine whether the DLL has been hooked. Then, overwrite the hooked code with code from a clean DLL (from disk / Windows cache) to restore the API to its original state. At this point, even if something in the DLL is executed, the EDR will not see it.

Many techniques have been developed since then. I may add more when I have time, but this is essentially how a basic unhook works.

ref:

  • https://www.ired.team/offensive-security/defense-evasion/how-to-unhook-a-dll-using-c++
  • https://docs.redteamleaders.com/offensive-security/defense-evasion/hookchain-technique-introduction-by-helvio-junior-m4v3r1ck
  • https://github.com/EvilBytecode/Nyx-Full-Dll-Unhook
  • https://github.com/trickster0/LdrLoadDll-Unhooking
    • https://killer.wtf/2022/01/19/CustomJmpUnhook.html
    • https://www.cnblogs.com/fdxsec/p/18146252

Direct Syscalls

Call syscalls directly, without going through a hooked DLL such as ntdll.dll to execute those important functions.

  • https://github.com/jthuraisamy/SysWhispers2
  • https://github.com/klezVirus/SysWhispers3
  • https://github.com/am0nsec/HellsGate

This requires reading addresses from the loaded ntdll.dll and dynamically calculating the syscall number and system service numbers (SSN), so the code does not need to be rewritten for every version.

However, there is still a chance of leaving traces and being detected because:

  • The syscall instruction executes outside the memory of ntdll.dll, which is unusual.
  • The return instruction does as well.

Both of these are considered non-legitimate on Windows.

Indirect Syscalls

Use the Native APIs in ntdll.dll, such as NtOpenProcess and NtWriteVirtualMemory, to make system calls without going through higher-level DLLs such as kernel32.dll.

Because execution occurs directly in the memory of ntdll.dll, and the return also occurs in ntdll.dll memory before pointing to the indirect syscall assembly that actually needs to execute, the disadvantages of direct syscalls mentioned above are resolved. However, if the EDR uses ETW (Event Tracing for Windows), it may still discover anomalies through the call stack.

However, if ntdll.dll itself has also been hooked, attempting to use ntdll.dll to perform an indirect syscall will still be visible to the EDR.

ref: https://0xdarkvortex.dev/hiding-in-plainsight/

Reference

https://www.ired.team/offensive-security/defense-evasion/how-to-unhook-a-dll-using-c++

https://redops.at/en/blog/direct-syscalls-vs-indirect-syscalls

https://docs.redteamleaders.com/offensive-security/defense-evasion/hookchain-technique-introduction-by-helvio-junior-m4v3r1ck

entry.title: SEKAI CTF 2022 writeup
entry.content:
This is my first time writing a writeup as a blog post. The interface for this competition was really cute, and as a Project Sekai player, I felt that I had to participate somehow. I also happened to encounter a challenge that I found quite interesting. At first, I thought it would be unlikely that I could solve it during the competition, but I luckily managed to solve it later. I ended up solving two easy challenges in total, so I am recording them here. The challenges are still available; I will add more if there are any updates.

Bottle Poem

http://bottle-poem.ctf.sekai.team 146/852 solve

The page for this challenge looks like this. There are several links in the middle of the page. Clicking a link takes you to a URL like http://bottle-poem.ctf.sekai.team/show?id=spring.txt, which retrieves the corresponding poem’s txt file and displays it on the page.

The /show?id= endpoint looked like it might allow file reading, and using id=/etc/passwd did indeed retrieve the file. After looking around, I found that:

  • If the file does not exist, it displays No This Poems.
  • id=/proc/self/cmdline displays python3.
  • id=../app.py displays No!!!!

At this point, I could infer that it was probably running on a Python web framework similar to Flask, so I wanted to see whether I could retrieve some source code that Flask might have. Although using ../app.py returned No!!!!, using id=/app/app.py could actually retrieve the source.

Now it was clear why ../app.py returned No!!!!. At this point, I wondered whether I needed to log in as admin. Logging in as admin was actually quite simple, because it only checked the value of "name" in the cookie. I just needed to retrieve the secret with id=/app/config/secret.py and sign a cookie satisfying session["name"] == "admin". However, things were of course not that simple: visiting the /sign page with the admin cookie only produced a page like this.

Before trying this, I could already have realized that it was a dead end by using id=/app/views/admin.html (although it did not take much effort). While wondering what this challenge actually wanted us to do, I remembered that the format of this cookie looked somewhat like JSON. Could it have something to do with unserialize again? After searching for a while, I found Python Web Framework Session Management: From LFR to RCE (I found a translation, but I could not find the original article… I will add it if I find it). It happened to discuss the Bottle framework. After looking through the source, I saw that its get_cookie function uses pickle.loads to process this cookie! The answer was then obvious: use unpickle RCE.

Finally, I made a simple script based on the source to generate the cookie and prepared to receive a reverse shell. This challenge required executing a file in the root directory to print the flag, so that was it.

Sekai Game Start

http://sekai-game-start.ctf.sekai.team 63/852 solve

This was a PHP challenge that directly showed us the source code. In short, we needed to send it a serialized string. Clearly, it had to be a serialized string for Sekai_Game, and when Sekai_Game reached __destruct, $start had to be true in order to obtain the flag.

There were two key points in this challenge:

  • How to send the "sekai_game.run" parameter.
  • How to bypass the __wakeup function.

The first point was a problem because when passing GET parameters to PHP, . is automatically converted into an underscore. No matter how it was sent, it was therefore impossible to provide the parameter correctly. This parameter was arguably not a particularly valid one either. However, after looking into the source code for this version (php 7.4.5), I found a section in main/php_variables.c that performs these conversions. I then discovered that when PHP encounters the character [, it treats it as an array and performs the subsequent array-related checks. However, if it cannot find a closing ], it converts the [ into _ and stops. Most importantly, it does nothing else, including checking the characters that follow. Therefore, when we send sekai[game.run, it is ultimately converted into the sekai_game.run we need.

HexRabbit initially looked at the wrong version. This part had already been fixed, so they could not find this solution for a long time, but they did learn that it had later been changed XD

The second problem was how to bypass __wakeup. For Sekai_Game‘s start to be true, execution must not enter __wakeup. I found PHP Bug #81151 bypass __wakeup, where the object used "C" rather than "O" in the serialized string. In the bug report, the author said:

In my understand, “C:” means a class implements Serializable, and it don’t suport __wakeup.

I am not sure whether this is correct, and the author was not sure either, but constructing the payload this way did work (it does not work on php8). Thus, the final solution was:

If we provided additional parameters for Sekai_Game here, however, __wakeup would execute normally, as in:

But if we added the old method for bypassing __wakeup (CVE-2016-7124, PHP5 < 5.6.25/PHP7 < 7.0.10), we could bypass it again.

I do not understand it either, but that is how it worked. This challenge was a double dose of obscure tricks. When I could not solve it, I felt completely stuck, because I was fairly sure it must be testing some kind of obscure trick XD. However, I really wanted to know the solution and could not wait until the competition ended, so I asked people about it everywhere. Fortunately, I still managed to solve it myself before the end. After solving these two challenges, though, I did not have much energy left to look at the others. My patience and stamina are really limited, but I hope I can continue improving little by little.

entry.title: PACMAN: Attacking ARM Pointer Authentication with Speculative Execution
entry.content:
paper: https://pacmanattack.com/paper.pdf

Abstract

This paper proposes a new attack called PACMAN. It combines memory corruption vulnerabilities with speculative execution vulnerabilities, using side channels to speculatively leak the result of PAC verification without causing a crash. The attack was successfully demonstrated on the Apple M1 SoC, the first personal-computer processor to support ARM Pointer Authentication.

Introduction

PACMAN is primarily a hardware-related attack. Previous vulnerabilities such as Meltdown and Spectre were also hardware-related. PACMAN mainly targets the speculative execution feature to bypass ARM pointer authentication.

ARM Pointer Authentication

When carrying out memory-related attacks, attackers often need to control data pointers and then control the execution flow. ARM therefore provides Pointer Authentication (PA) to protect pointers from being modified. This protection makes it difficult to tamper with a pointer without being detected.

In general, the actual address space on a 64-bit architecture is smaller than 64 bits, so the unused bits can be used to store a hash value—a Pointer Authentication Code (PAC)—to protect the pointer. If the PAC is incorrect when the pointer is used, the program crashes.

A PAC can be as small as 11 bits or as large as 31 bits, depending on the system configuration. However, even a small PAC is not easy to brute-force, because after a crash and restart, a new secret key is used, and crashing too frequently is also easy to detect.

Key Challenge

The research challenges on Apple platforms were:

  • Very little public documentation exists about their microarchitecture.
  • By default, high-resolution timers are not exposed to userspace.
    • (Such timers are said to be very important for microarchitectural reverse engineering.)

Contributions

  • Propose the PACMAN attack.
  • Develop microarchitectural timing side-channel attack primitives and a reverse-engineering tool for Apple M1 processors.
  • Reverse-engineer the TLB organization and perform the first TLB-based side-channel attack using speculative execution on Apple M1 processors.
  • Show that the PACMAN attack works across privilege levels. (We demonstrate several proof-of-concept PACMAN attacks, including constructing PAC oracles, brute-forcing PACs, and a control-flow hijacking attack targeting a PA-enabled kernel module.)

Impact

  • Industry: It can affect all ARM processors that use existing PAC designs.
  • Academia: Many papers and assumptions based on memory-safety premises can be invalidated, making it necessary to modify and reevaluate the threat model.
  • Highlights that security mechanisms employing a security-by-crash design principle and relying on a low collision probability are potentially vulnerable to speculative execution attacks.
  • Speculation can serve as a primitive for suppressing crashes.

Background

Memory Corruption Vulnerabilities

These vulnerabilities occur in software written in low-level languages, including:

  • out-of-bound writes
  • out-of-bound reads
  • use-after-free
  • double-free bugs
  • integer overflows and underflows
  • size confusion attacks
  • type confusion attacks

They can modify or destroy data and code pointers in memory. Modifying a code pointer can change the program’s execution flow and cause serious consequences. This is also known as a control-flow hijacking attack; ROP and JOP are examples.

Common protections include:

  • stack canaries
  • data execution prevention
  • ASLR
  • kASLR (kernel ASLR)

Although these protections increase the difficulty of attacks, they can still potentially be bypassed.

ARM Pointer Authentication

ARMv8.3 introduced PA as a low-overhead protection mechanism to prevent pointers from being modified. It primarily protects pointers by signing them with a hash, called a Pointer Authentication Code (PAC). The PAC is checked before the pointer is used.

Signing and Verifying Pointers

In practice, a 64-bit architecture does not use the entire 64-bit address space. PA stores the PAC in the unused bits.

The context value used to generate the hash shown in the figure contains a key in a register accessible only at a higher privilege level, as well as a program-specified salt.

ISA Extension


To provide PA functionality, PA provides two groups of instruction sets for these operations:

  • Instructions beginning with pac perform signing.
    • The hardware can keep up to five keys recorded simultaneously. The key used for a particular signing operation is determined by the opcode.
    • e.g. pacia ptr, salt
  • Instructions beginning with aut perform verification.

On Apple chips, in addition to protecting return addresses, PAC is also used to protect many other data structures, including C++ vtable pointers, vtable entries, and Objective-C method caches.

Microarchitectural Side Channels

Shared microarchitectural structures, including caches, TLBs, functional units, and networks-on-chip, can be used to leak sensitive information.

Prime+Probe

  • Has relatively few restrictions.
  • The attacker first fills the cache. After the victim accesses it, the attacker accesses the entire cache again and uses timing differences to determine which parts the victim accessed.

Flush+Reload

  • Requires shared memory.
  • The attacker first flushes the memory locations to be observed. After the victim finishes executing, the attacker scans the memory again and uses timing differences to determine which locations were accessed.
  • Used by both Meltdown and Spectre.

Evict+Reload

  • Requires shared memory.
  • Similar to Prime+Probe, but operates on shared memory.

Speculative Execution Attacks

Speculative execution is a processor optimization. Because processors operate very quickly, they execute ahead in order to make better use of their resources. For example, with branch prediction, the processor guesses which path a branch will take before the branch condition is determined and begins executing that path. If the prediction is correct, execution can continue directly; if it is incorrect, the processor returns to the branch point and takes the correct path. However, this optimization has also introduced several vulnerabilities.

Meltdown

Meltdown exploits exceptions and speculative execution. Before execution stops due to an exception, the processor speculatively runs ahead to instructions that load sensitive information and then stops.

Spectre

Spectre targets conditional branches or indirect branches.

Threat Model

  • Target
    • Use a PAC oracle on a PA-enabled victim to recover the PAC and achieve a control-flow hijacking attack.
  • Attacker
    • An unprivileged userspace application.
  • Victim
    • The operating system kernel.
  • Assumptions
    1. The victim program contains an exploitable memory corruption vulnerability that allows the attacker to write arbitrary data to memory.
    2. PA is enabled and PACMAN gadgets exist.
    3. A side-channel attack can be performed (that is, a high-resolution timer is available).

The PACMAN Attack

The main idea is to use speculative execution attacks and microarchitectural side channels to leak the result of PAC verification without causing a crash.

PACMAN gadgets

Some exploitable code patterns are referred to as PACMAN gadgets. They consist of two operations:

  • verification
    Verifies the PAC. Given a pointer, it checks whether the PAC is correct. If it is correct, it outputs a valid pointer; if it is incorrect, it outputs an invalid pointer, which causes an execution error, as described in the Background section.
  • transmission
    Speculatively executes the verified output pointer. This may involve a load or store—in other words, the pointer is speculatively translated into a physical address and used. If execution succeeds, it produces an observable side effect that can be monitored through a side channel to leak relevant information. If speculative execution fails, it produces a speculative exception. Because these events occur under a mis-speculated branch, they do not cause a crash.

PACMAN gadgets are further divided into the following two types:

  • Data PACMAN Gadget (Figure 3c)
    • Caused by speculatively predicting a branch and performing data accesses.
    • AUT: pointer authentication instruction.
    • guessed_ptr: pointer provided by the attacker.
    • verified_ptr: output pointer from AUT.
    • Whether the pointer is correct can be determined by observing the difference between a load being executed and an exception occurring.
  • Instruction PACMAN Gadget (Figure 3d)
    • Caused by speculatively predicting a branch and performing instruction fetches.
    • Before AUT completes, the branch target buffer (BTB) predicts BR2. (This is common in nested-branch prediction.)
    • After AUT completes and determines that the BR2 prediction was incorrect, it eagerly squashes BR2.
    • It fetches the correct BR2, which is the result of AUT.
    • Limitations:
      • The processor must support eager squashing of nested branches. There must be a third step that squashes the pointer after AUT; only then will the pointer be used and the result of AUT can be leaked.
      • It must be possible to distinguish the side effects of fetching the verified pointer from those of the BTB prediction. In the TLB-based side channel used by this proof of concept, the BTB prediction and the verified pointer must be on different pages.

Gadget Detection

Using Ghidra’s scripting API, conditional branches in the kernel are located and the following 32 instructions are inspected. If the verified pointer is used in a transmit instruction—a memory access or a branch instruction—it is considered a PACMAN gadget.

In xnu-8019.80.24, 13,867 data PACMAN gadgets and 41,292 instruction PACMAN gadgets were found. Because only the following 32 instructions were searched, there may be even more gadgets if a larger range is examined.

An End-to-End Illustrative Example


Suppose there is a BoF that can overwrite a function pointer.

  1. Execute the program normally and train the BTB and branch predictor (cond = true).
  2. Use the BoF to modify fp, then guess the PAC until it is correct (cond = false; the branch is not actually taken, but is speculatively executed, so no crash occurs).
  3. Finally, use the guessed PAC to complete the exploit (con = true).

Attack Platform

  • Apple M1 SoC
    • The first desktop aarch64 platform supporting ARMv8.3 extensions, including PA.
    • EL0: the execution level for usermode programs.
    • EL1: the execution level for the kernel.
  • macOS and the XNU Kernel
    • OS: macOS
    • XNU Kernel
      • Has loadable kernel extensions, or kexts.
      • Used later during reverse engineering.

None of the above is open source, and there is little documentation, so reverse engineering is needed to obtain the required information. This is also one of the paper’s major contributions.

Reverse Engineering Tools

High-Resolution Timers

As mentioned earlier, side-channel attacks such as Prime+Probe require precise timing, so the researchers identified which timers in the M1 could be used.

  • CNTPCT_EL0
    • System Counter. All cores share this counter, but its frequency of 24 MHz is too low to precisely observe differences such as cache hits and misses.
  • PMCCNTR_EL0
    • ARM Cycle Count Register. Most ARM Cortex processors have performance monitoring units (PMUs) and therefore provide this counter, but the M1’s PMU is not a standard PMU, so it does not provide it.
  • PMC0
    • This counter is not mentioned in the documentation and counts cycles. There is also a PMC1 that counts instructions, but neither is accessible from userspace.
    • To use it, the researchers used the previously mentioned kext to modify a control register, PMCR0, so that PMC0 could be accessed from userspace. (This was only for reverse engineering and was not used in the attack.)
  • Custom Multi-thread Timer
    • The researchers implemented a userspace-accessible timer that does not require a kext, as follows:
    • isb is used for control flow, but they later found that omitting it slightly increased variation while providing greater timing precision, so they ultimately removed it.

PacmanOS

Written in Rust, this is a bare-metal environment that can run on the M1. It gives the researchers complete control over the environment, including the hardware and other sources of interference, making experiments easier to conduct.

Reverse Engineering

Basic Memory Hierarchy Information

The M1 uses a big.LITTLE design.

big.LITTLE: A combination proposed by ARM that combines more powerful big cores with weaker but more power-efficient little cores. Here, the terms p-core (Performance) and e-core (Efficient) are used for big and little, respectively, although these are Intel’s naming conventions.

The M1 memory system has two levels of cache, with different sizes on different cores. The kernel uses 48-bit virtual addresses and a 16-bit PAC.

L1 Data TLB and L2 TLB

The researchers mainly studied p-core behavior because speculative behavior on p-cores is more reliable. Unlike Linux, which provides an API (taskset) to directly specify which core should execute a task, they used pthread_set_qos_class_self_np to “suggest” to the kernel which core to use. The counter they used was PMC0, which requires a kext.

The experiment used Prime+Probe to measure the TLB size. The main steps were:

  1. Load a particular address.
  2. Load N addresses to fill the TLB.
  3. Load the address from step 1 again and measure the latency.

The result was Figure (a). Each gap represents the boundary of a TLB size (L1 dTLB/L2 TLB). Although this cannot conclusively prove that the cache organization is exactly as inferred, it does reveal how to fill the TLB.

TLB conflicts and cache conflicts were measured using different methods for calculating the addresses of the N loaded addresses, producing Figure (b) (L1 cache/L2 cache/L1 dTLB/L2 TLB).

L1 Instruction TLB

  1. Fill both the L1 dTLB and the L2 TLB.
  2. Branch to a particular address.
  3. Execute N branches to fill the iTLB (called the instruction eviction set).
  4. Load the address from step 2 and measure the latency. (The reason for using a “load” to obtain data-access latency is explained below.)

The result was Figure (c). Before explaining the result, the inferred overall TLB organization is described below.

  • The user and kernel L1 iTLBs are not shared, so userspace cannot observe differences in kernel space.
  • The L1 dTLB is a non-inclusive backing store for the L1 iTLB. When the iTLB is filled, entries are also placed in the dTLB. This is why step 4 above uses a “load” to measure data-access latency.

Summary of Reverse Engineering Results

  • After filling the iTLB, the dTLB can also be filled.

  • Both PMC0 and the Multi-thread Counter can clearly distinguish between TLB hits and misses, as well as cache hits and misses.

Proof-of-Concept Attacks

PAC Oracles

In the experiment, the researchers installed a kext containing a syscall that could trigger a PACMAN gadget. They then tested a large number of pointers with correct PACs and pointers without PACs, measuring the timing with the counter they defined. They used both data accesses and instruction fetches to leak whether the PAC was correct.

  • Leaking via Data Accesses
    • Because the dTLB is shared between userspace and the kernel, it can be measured directly.
    1. Train the PACMAN gadget’s branch predictor (64 times).
    2. Reset the TLB.
    3. Prime the L1 dTLB.
    4. Trigger the PACMAN gadget by passing in the pointer containing the PAC to be tested.
    5. Probe the L1 dTLB set by re-accessing the eviction set and report the number of L1 dTLB misses.
  • Leaking via Instruction Fetches
    • The kernelspace and userspace L1 iTLBs are not shared. Therefore, userspace triggers self-conflicts in kernelspace and fills its iTLB, thereby filling the shared dTLB.
    • The preceding steps are the same as for data accesses.
    1. Use the set that filled the iTLB to attempt to fill it again.
    2. Finally, check whether it was also placed in the dTLB to determine whether a miss occurred.

Brute-Force Attack

  • Attack Speed
    • The M1 uses a 16-bit PAC.
    • It takes 2.94 minutes on average to try all possible PAC values.
    • The main time cost is the syscall used to train the predictor. This could be shortened, but it is not necessary.
  • Attack Accuracy
    • Noisy environment.
    • 90% correct PAC (45).
    • 10% no PAC value was found (5).
    • No false positives (incorrect PACs).

Jump2Win Attack

Once the PAC is available, the vulnerability can be exploited directly.

Countermeasures

  • Explore PAC-agnostic execution.
    • Modify the architecture or software to ensure that PACs are not verified and used during speculation.
    • Pause speculative execution when a memory access or branch requires a verified pointer.
      • fence/isb
      • This reduces performance.
    • Always assume that the PAC will pass during speculative execution.
      • Speculatively executing with invalid pointers may cause a Meltdown-style vulnerability.
      • This must be combined with Meltdown mitigations.
  • Improve Spectre defenses.
    • Make speculative loads unobservable.
      • Invisible speculation mechanisms.
      • Such as InvisiSpec, SafeSpec, and Delay-on-Miss.
    • Use information-flow tracking to prevent secrets accessed speculatively from being leaked.
      • STT, NDA, and Dolma.
      • Taint pointer authentication instructions.
  • Do not write programs containing memory corruption vulnerabilities.

entry.title: CVE-2021-3129 Laravel debug mode: Remote code execution
entry.content:
Environment

  • Docker Ubuntu 20.04.3

    • How to Check & Install Specific version of PHP in Ubuntu Linux

      Composer

    Laravel

  • service apache2 restart
  • Add a route to routes/web.php following the format already used there, and you will be able to see the error page.

Analysis

After clicking Make variable optional, a POST request is sent to /public/index.php/_ignition/execute-solution, with the following data:

Searching for execute-solution leads to the following code in vendor/facade/ignition/src/
IgnitionServiceProvider.php:

Continue by locating vendor/facade/ignition/src/Http/Controllers/ExecuteSolutionController.php.

vendor/facade/ignition/src/Http/Requests/ExecuteSolutionRequest.php

At this point, we can see that this solution is the one specified in the request above:

Continuing the search leads to
vendor/facade/ignition/src/Solutions/MakeViewVariableOptionalSolution.php.

It changes the original $<variableName> to $<variableName> ?? '' and writes it back to the page. Here, variableName is the username from the request above. The large amount of code in generateExpectedTokens is actually just checking whether $<variableName> ?? '' was generated as expected. Therefore, the vulnerability description article also mentions that it can be simplified as follows:

At this point, we can use file_get_contents to obtain a file containing the payload and then write it out. However, we need somewhere to write the payload. If there is an opportunity to upload a file, we can simply use phpggc to construct the payload (monolog/rce1 can be used), and then exploit it directly by using the phar:// protocol in viewFile.

When that is not possible, Laravel’s default log at storage/logs/laravel.log is a location that may be controllable. Send a POST request to see whether we can write something to it.


It works. However, to make subsequent file writing easier, it is better to clear the entire log first. My first instinct was also to use multiple rounds of base64 decoding to clear it. The disclosure article initially took the same approach, but problems arise:

After applying decoding three times, an ErrorException appeared. Checking the log again showed that it had not been successfully cleared. Testing revealed that the problem was caused by =. The presence of = can cause problems; after multiple rounds of base64 decoding, = will eventually appear, making it extremely difficult to control.

Therefore, the article says that they went back to look for another filter that could be used. It says that the consumed filter can clear the file, but I searched through the PHP documentation and could not find where this came from. Later, I found an article that used another method. Since = causes problems, first make all the contents non-base64 characters and then apply base64 decoding; naturally, everything will disappear. The method used is UTF-8 -> UTF-16BE -> printable -> UTF-8.

This successfully clears the log. The remaining question is how to preserve the written payload. From the log format observed during the previous test, two more issues need to be handled:

  1. The prefix at the beginning
  2. The payload appears twiceThe original article’s method is to first pass the data through convert.iconv.utf16le.utf-8. Padding the normal payload with null bytes filters out the non-UTF-16LE characters that were not padded.

During experimentation, we can also find that conversion will not work correctly without proper padding. The article cleverly adds one byte to the payload to misalign it, placing an odd number of bytes between the two payloads. This successfully handles the padding issue and also solves the problem of the payload appearing twice: the first occurrence is not aligned successfully, while the second one is aligned.

But two more problems appear at this point:

  1. The warning that also appeared in the earlier test
  2. Null bytes also cause a warning when passed through file_get_contents

The first problem can be solved by writing the padding once first, so that the prefix, midfix, and suffix each appear an even number of times:

For the second problem, the article suggests replacing null bytes with =00 and then passing them through convert.quoted-printable-decode, which allows them to pass through safely. Therefore, the final payload is base64 -> utf16le -> null to =00, and then passes back through this filter:

POC

  1. Clear the error log

    Or

  2. First send a request to ensure alignment

    When sending the first request used for alignment, the log generated after the payload is sent will contain the error failed to open stream: File name too long. Making the "viewFile" value in the first payload longer so that it produces the same error makes it less likely to fail ("viewFile" will produce failed to open stream: No such file or directory if it is shorter).

  3. Generate the payload using phpgcc mentioned earlier.

  4. After base64-encoding it, add padding to convert it to utf16le, then replace the null bytes with =00. Either Laravel/RCE8 or monolog/rce1 can be used here.

  5. Send the payload to be written into error.log.

    During testing, the error stream filter (convert.quoted-printable-decode): invalid byte sequence kept appearing. It turned out that part of the payload also appeared in the log’s stack trace. Sending only the payload directly caused an error.

    Therefore, at this step, it was discovered that some garbage must be added to the beginning of the payload to prevent the converted payload below from causing problems for the filter. It is recommended that more than 15 odd-numbered characters of garbage be added.

  6. Decode the payload and remove the garbage outside the payload.

  7. Use phar:// to trigger the payload.

    The file is successfully written.

Other

entry.title: Saphire: Sandboxing PHP Applications with Tailored System Call Allowlists
entry.content:
paper: https://www.usenix.org/system/files/sec21-bulekov.pdf

Abstract

  • PHP and Python are interpreted languages. Applications written in these languages often run with the same excessive privileges, violating the Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP)—that is, the principle that fewer privileges are better. This exposes the entire system to danger: once an RCE occurs, it is easy for an attacker to obtain overly high privileges and expose the system to even greater risks.
  • This paper aims to implement PoLP by properly controlling privileges, using the authors’ proposed method of automatically generating a syscall policy for each individual program.

Background

  • RCE
  • seccomp
    • Specifies that a process may call only particular system calls
  • ptrace
    • Allows a tracing process to observe or control the contents (such as memory or registers) or execution flow of another traced process
    • Primarily used to implement debuggers or trace syscalls

Overview

Interpreters

  • Interpreted program: a program that requires an interpreter to execute
  • An interpreter can be directly executed by the OS and hardware

Therefore, interpreted programs are portable. An interpreted program typically provides users with an API composed of several functions, and only these APIs can access syscalls. Even when JIT is used, syscalls can still be called only through the API.

An API for all interpreted programs

Because these APIs generally need to be highly general-purpose, they usually use many syscalls at once, so simply filtering syscalls is not meaningful. However, a program may use only a small subset of syscalls, in which case filtering can be useful.

For example, Prog1 does not need syscall1, so it can be filtered out.

Securing Interpreted Programs

  • Mapping the interpreter API to syscalls
    Use static and dynamic analysis to map API function handlers to syscalls
  • Identifying API calls within an interpreted program
    Identify the functions used in each piece of code, including all dependencies (both implicit and explicit), and then use the preceding mapping results to generate an allowed list
  • Protecting the Program
    Apply the allowed list to the program

Implementation

The steps mentioned above are implemented and explained using PHP here.

Mapping built-in PHP functions to system-calls

Map PHP functions to the system calls they use.

  • First, use static call-graph analysis to perform an initial mapping.
  • Then, use ptrace to observe the syscalls used while running the PHP process.

Static analysis over the PHP Interpreter

  • Use symbols to construct the static call graph of the entire interpreter and libraries (each node is a function, and each edge is a direct function call).
  • To find all handlers, use get_defined_functions() to locate the addresses of all built-in PHP function handlers.

Although this step is static, it must be run across many code bases (after examining the code, the paper also states that this takes more than 30 minutes).

Refining the mapping through dynamic analysis

Although the previous step exhaustively scanned the code in the entire PHP process, it misses indirect calls. For example, PHP’s fopen can access remote files, and some functions such as mail() execute the sendmail binary. Purely static analysis cannot map the syscalls invoked by sendmail.

  • TE finds the name of the PHP function currently running in shared memory.
  • TR uses ptrace to intercept syscalls.

Combining these two makes it possible to dynamically map this kind of function.

Creating system-call filters for web apps

The purpose of this step is to identify which PHP built-in functions the interpreter will invoke, and then compare them with the mapping table generated in the previous step to generate the system calls that each script in the web app may call.

  • First, iterate through all PHP files in the web app.
    • Use php-parser to generate an Abstract syntax tree (AST).
    • Scan the AST to identify possible built-in function calls.
    • Check assignments to determine class types and thereby map the functions.
  • Identify dependencies in the AST.
    • constant definitions
    • class definitions/instantiations
    • include/require operations

The most labor-intensive part is handling dependencies. Simple includes can be handled easily, but if variables or constants are used, additional processing is required.

String representation

Various methods are used to convert include strings of different kinds until they can no longer be processed or processing is complete.

(If a variable is assigned multiple times, each assignment is identified; if this is not possible, all possibilities are listed.)

Unresolved Includes

At this point, 74% of includes can be resolved. The remainder can be fuzzy resolved, meaning that a small set of contents is treated as having been included.

Some includes provide no information at all through static analysis. In this case, they provide a Conservative Includes option, which uses this method. After enabling this option, the probability of FP decreases, but the contents of the allowed list become more extensive.

Building system-call profiles for Scripts

Finally, once we have a script, the PHP functions that it and its dependencies will call, and the mapping obtained in the previous step, we can generate a profile mapping the script to its syscalls (script path <-> profile).

Sandboxing the Interpreter and Web App

This allowed list is implemented using seccomp. This SE extension determines which script the process is running when it starts and tells the kernel which syscall allowed list to use.

Therefore, this SE runs twice during the lifetime of an interpreter. The first time is when the PHP process starts, when all allowed lists are loaded into memory. When a request is received, the applicable allowed list is sent to the kernel.

(libseccomp is used to convert a sequence of syscalls into an allowlist.)

  • Web requests are usually handled by a web server such as nginx or Apache, so this plugin is installed on the web server as well as in the PHP CLI API (the command-line interface).
  • Because seccomp is used, a process can run only one script (a process cannot suddenly switch to a different allowed list).
    • A PHP interpreter process can be used for only one request, but this approach results in very high latency when loading is expensive.
    • Each PHP worker can handle many requests, but the same worker can handle requests for only the same script.

Evaluation

Dependency Resolution

  • All dependencies are divided into those that can be resolved literally and those that require dynamic resolution.
  • Resolved avg -> 74%
  • Fuzzy resolved -> 22%
  • Class 85%
  • For example, Joolma changes many original classes to call them using aliases, which cannot be detected in this case.

Syscall Profile Size

  • To understand how many syscalls are filtered and how effective CI is, examine the size of the syscall profile. The larger the size, the more syscalls are available, so it should be kept as small as possible while still allowing the program to run.
  • Dangerous syscalls were also evaluated in particular.
  • The black line represents the state when CI is not enabled.
    • When it is enabled, FP decreases, but the danger increases.
  • Approximately 80% of dangerous system calls are filtered.
  • Some common functions appear in many scripts, making the profiles of many scripts very similar.

Defense Capabilities

  • 21 RCE exploits were selected for testing.
  • Is too restrictive?
    • Calculate coverage to demonstrate that the program executes normally.
    • After enabling CI, there is no FP at all.
    • After disabling it:
      • Joomla is affected by the alias issue mentioned above.
  • Payload constraint?
    • The dangerous syscalls remaining after filtering are insufficient to construct a payload capable of ACE. They also performed many additional tests and found that the remaining syscalls lacked the components needed to assemble a payload.
  • Non-vuln plugins
    • Non-vulnerable plugins were also tested to evaluate FP.
  • Runtime Overhead
    • The key issue arises after implementation in the web app. Because of the seccomp issue mentioned above, the process must be restarted after each request is processed.
    • The resulting overhead is small enough to be negligible. Even particularly trivial scripts are not affected significantly. In particular, after implementing the method whereby “the same worker can handle requests for only the same script,” the impact is even smaller.

Limitations and Discussion

  • eval() system()
    • They do not handle these two functions or their arguments.
  • Mimicry
    • Although the results are already very good and no RCE occurred in the tests, some dangerous syscalls are still allowed and may be combined into a payload.
  • Overwriting scripts
    • If an attacker can modify a script and mislead the profile, this can be addressed simply by using a checksum.
  • Writing to sensitive files
    • To prevent attackers from gaining privileges by writing files, ptrace is also used to ensure that the interpreter cannot access certain important fds (file descriptors).
  • Installing plugins
    • When a new plugin is installed, a profile is immediately created for it, but this requires manual action.
  • Filter system call argument
    • In addition to directly filtering syscalls, filtering their arguments as well would provide greater precision.
  • Line coverage of evaluated web apps
  • Applying Saphire to other interpreters
    • Python interpreter running a program composed of multiple python scripts
    • A server executing multiple Node.JS microservices
    • classic CGI-based interpreted web-app using a language such as Perl or Lua

entry.title: HITCON 2018 One Line PHP Challenge
entry.content:
This is orange’s one-line PHP challenge. Every year, he creates a challenge like this one. This challenge primarily makes use of session.upload_progress.

P.S. This is a default installation PHP7.2 + Apache on Ubuntu 18.04

session.upload_progress

  • enabled
    When session.upload_progress.enabled=On (in /etc/php/7.4/apache2/php.ini), some information about uploaded files is stored in the session (the session location is /var/lib/php/sessions), so it can be useful when performing LFI.
  • cleanup
    When session.upload_progress.cleanup is enabled, the session file is deleted as soon as the file upload is complete.
  • name、prefix In addition, name is controllable. As long as this value is included in the POST request, we can successfully control the name. This prefix + name becomes the key used when storing the session. It is explained in detail in the documentation.

    session

  • auto_start
    If session.auto_start=On is enabled, a session is created automatically. Otherwise, session_start() must be called. It is disabled by default :( However, if you include PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS and PHPSESSID, it will create a session for you.
  • session.use_strict_mode
    When this is Off, PHPSESSID can be defined manually.

    Experiment

Problem

Returning to the challenge itself, let’s first experiment with how the session works (first disable cleanup for easier observation).

The challenge reads the beginning of the file. Although the portion after upload_progress_*** in the filename can already be controlled, the prefix at the beginning still needs to be handled. This can be done by repeatedly applying base64 decoding to remove it. Base64 only processes characters that it can handle; characters it cannot handle are ignored. Therefore, if a string is decoded repeatedly, it will eventually disappear.

  • For example, taking the string inside orange as an example, decoding upload_progress_ZZ once leaves the four valid characters hikY; decoding it once more leaves nothing that can be decoded, so performing three decodes makes the entire string disappear. Note that the result after each operation must be a multiple of 4; otherwise, it will consume the payload we want to preserve. This is why the string ZZ is used here: it happens to be exactly the right length.

Finally, this method can be used by encoding the payload three times and prepending ZZ (note that the payload cannot contain =, so some additional padding is needed). I originally got this wrong, thinking that the payload afterward would affect the number of decodes required, but it actually does not. Thanks to splitline for the correction.

Also, because auto_start is not enabled and session_start is not used, it might seem that this would be a problem. However, as mentioned earlier, it is not. Since session.upload_progress.cleanup is enabled, a race condition is required to win the race against deletion.
Finally, here is orange’s exploit.

References

  • official writeup
  • orange github
  • HITCON 2018 Notes on Being Tortured, Part One: One-Line PHP Challenge Study
  • manual session.upload-progress
  • Implementing RCE with PHP session.upload_process + LFI

entry.title: CVE-2019-14287 linux sudo root
entry.content:
MITRE CVE-2019-14287

  • Sudo before 1.8.28
  • The current identity has sudo privileges

Background

  • Running sudo -l lists entries in a format such as the following:
    • (as user: as group) nopassword:commands
    • For example, (ALL:!root) /bin/bash means that /bin/bash can be executed as any user and as any group except root. This can be used to switch identities and execute commands.
    • (ALL:ALL) /bin/ping allows you to run sudo -u#1234 /bin/ping to execute ping as the user with user ID 1234.

Cause

The main issue occurs in the setresuid system call. Its code can be found in sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/i386/setresuid.c. One section of the code checks whether the passed-in ruid, euid, and suid are equal to -1. If they are not equal, it assigns these values; otherwise, it retains the default value of 0 (that is, root), which causes this issue.

In the patch, an additional check was added in sudo’s lib/util/strtoid.c to prevent id == -1 or UINT_MAX (4294967295) (line 76).

PoC

Using sudo -u#-1 <executable command> allows privilege escalation.

Reference

  • Sudo Vulnerability Cheat Sheet: Learn All About CVE-2019-14287
  • Linux su and sudo Command Tutorial and Examples
  • Analysis of CVE-2019-14287 (Linux sudo vulnerability)

entry.title: CVE-2021-21972 VMware vCenter Server
entry.content:
MITRE CVE-2021-21972

  • This is an RCE vulnerability in the vCenter Server plugin.
  • In other words, anyone who can access this machine’s web interface can trigger this vulnerability.
  • Affected versions
    • VMware vCenter Server
      • 7.x before 7.0 U1c
      • 6.7 before 6.7 U3l
      • 6.5 before 6.5 U3n
    • VMware Cloud Foundation
      • 4.x before 4.2
      • 5.3.x before 3.10.1.2

Cause

There is an API called uploadova that can upload OVA files (/ui/vropspluginui/rest/services/uploadova). If it receives a tar file, it extracts it into /tmp/unicorn_ova_dir. However, tar has a remarkable feature: it accepts filenames containing ../, so it is possible to access arbitrary other directories!

At this point, it is easy to figure out: upload a backdoor to the location you want, and you get RCE.

PoC

https://github.com/NS-Sp4ce/CVE-2021-21972

  • This PoC uses Ice Scorpion shellcode. As long as the malicious payload can be placed through this vulnerability in a location accessible from the web, a backdoor can be opened.
  • It first checks whether /ui/vropspluginui/rest/services/uploadova is enabled, using a 405 response to confirm whether the vulnerability is present. If it is, it brute-forces the variable in ../../usr/lib/vmware-vsphere-ui/server/work/deployer/s/global/[某個數字]/0/h5ngc.war/resources/shell.jsp to determine which one is exposed externally.
  • In practice, it used Shodan to scan machines in Taiwan with Vcenter country:TW and vSphere country:TW, and found that many were on academic networks and appeared to actually be vulnerable to attack.

Ice Scorpion webshell

  • The webshell seen in one of the PoCs encrypts the transmitted data, making it difficult to detect.
  • Red-versus-blue confrontation—offense and defense of the encrypted Webshell “Ice Scorpion”
  • At the beginning, it exchanges a 16-bit key, which is a relatively obvious characteristic.
  • Using dynamic binary encryption to implement a new type of one-line Trojan: PHP edition

entry.title: The Ninjutsu of Steganography
entry.content:
As a CTF noob, I can only start with misc challenges that other people might not even bother with and see whether I can pick up a few points. Recently, I thought I should become more familiar with the various Stego tricks so that the next time I try to pick up points, I at least won’t be unable to solve even the misc challenges. So I read some articles about Stego techniques and have organized them here briefly.

Hiding Files

This should be a relatively easy trick to discover: hide a file inside an image. The principle is that image-reading tools usually treat a file as a jpg when they encounter the ending 'FF D9', so they ignore any data after it. The image can therefore still be displayed normally, and changing the file extension to zip turns it back into an archive. I just thought it was interesting, so I am recording it here.

On Windows, you can create one directly with copy /b a.jpg+b.zip output.jpg; on Linux, you can use cat a.jpg b.zip > output.jpg.
When you encounter this, simply opening it with winhex will reveal that there is more data at the end. It can also be easily detected with binwalk.

If you need to extract the hidden content, or split apart content combined in the same file, there are several ways to do so.

  • In winhex, select the part you want to extract, then right-click and choose Edit->Copy Block->Into New File
  • dd dd if=[input] of=[output] skip=[ 從哪個byte開始做 ] bs=1
  • foremost foremost [pic]

LSB (Least Significant Bit)

Messages can be hidden in image data. I have encountered this in CTFs, and usually solve it directly with stegsolve. Each pixel consists of three primary colors, and each color uses 8 bits. If only the last bit is changed, it is usually difficult to notice, so a message can be hidden in the last bit. ASCII can be used, or only this one bit can be used to form different patterns and hide a message. This technique cannot be used with jpg because jpg compresses images, which may destroy the hidden message. PNG and BMP images may use this technique.
As an aside, when you encounter a QR code or barcode, you can scan it using this website.

File Repair

Sometimes the provided image is corrupted and needs to be repaired. In such cases, it is helpful to know a little about the structure of different file types, although often only the beginning is incorrect and it can simply be fixed with an editor.
Sometimes the image’s width and height need to be changed. Making them larger may reveal the hidden part.

  • PNG
  • GIF
  • JPG
  • Magic Number in File

Metadata

Sometimes a message is hidden directly in an image’s metadata. On Windows, you can view it directly by right-clicking and opening the properties. On Linux, you can use exiftool to inspect it, or upload it directly to an online service.
For example, picoCTF 2018’s Truly an Artist.

Two Images

When two images are provided, you usually need to compare the differences between them. The operation may be XOR/SUB/AND/OR/MUL or something else. You can make use of stegsolve’s Analysis->Image Combiner.
Sometimes you need to compare differences in the data and identify the problematic data segments for analysis.

Blind Watermark

Script and instructions
In addition to images, audio files, PDFs, and pcaps can also contain hidden content. If I encounter related challenges in the future, I will come back and add them here.

entry.content:
This was my first time working with anything related to OS, so I was extremely unfamiliar with it. I was worried that I would forget everything later, so I decided to document it.
I wrote this first assignment by referring to many senior students’ blogs and trying things out alongside them, orz. I still need to spend more time understanding the architecture.
I mainly referred to these two blogs:

Terry Nini OS::NachOS::HW1

Morris Blog: Working Toward NachOS 4.0 Assignments (1)

Initial Assignment

Install

It is said that this must be run on Ubuntu 14.04 (32-bit) or an older version; otherwise, additional patching is required. Anything newer than 14.04 really does cause problems. I initially downloaded 14.04.1 and got completely stuck.

Test

Then you can test whether it runs properly.
Enter the NachOS/code/userprog directory.

If everything is working properly, you should see output like this:

I also tried running two processes at the same time, as suggested online. (Remember to add test2 to the Makefile first, and then run make test2.)

MultiProgramming

Many blogs mentioned this problem, but I did not encounter it at first. I had just started congratulating myself for avoiding it when I encountered it while testing my Sleep() implementation. It was incredibly frustrating…

When I tried to run two Sleep() calls with different durations while alternating the use of PrintInt, I discovered that the two threads interfered with each other. The content that I intended to print only ten times was repeated nearly thirty times. Whenever the counter variable i was about to approach its ending value of 10, it would jump. It was obvious that the two threads were using the same block of memory, so I modified the code below based on Morris’s blog.

code/userprog/addrspace.h

code/usrprog/addrspace.cc

Add the following declaration and initialization:

Release the resources:

This part also needs to be modified in code/userprog/addrspace.cc.
The main tasks are to find available pages and calculate the entry point.

System Call Example

The slides contain an example implementation of a system call. By following the slides, you can implement a system call with functionality similar to PrintInt.
Add the definition and declaration to /code/userprog/syscall.h.

Add an example.c file to /code/test.

Then recompile NachOS. As before, add example to test/Makefile, run make example, and it should run.

For reference, the format in the Makefile looks like this:

Implement Sleep()

First, use the same method as when creating Example.
Add the definition and declaration to /code/userprog/ syscall.h.

The slides mention that we need to implement WaitUntil, so we can use WaitUntil to achieve the effect of Sleep.

/code/userprog/ exception.cc

Add the assembly to /code/test/start.s. Based on my understanding, this is not especially low-level assembly; it simply places the system call number we defined into $2 and then calls it.

Next, we need to complete WaitUntil. This function has already been declared in /code/threads/alarm.h; it needs to be implemented in /code/threads/alarm.cc.
However, because additional things are needed, /code/threads/alarm.h also needs to be modified.

/code/threads/alarm.cc

According to Morris’s blog, the kernel calls Alarm::CallBack() periodically. Therefore, PutToReady() is called there so that each invocation of CallBack() checks whether any threads should wake up. If there are, it removes them from the sleep list and places them in ReadyToRun.

Finally, write two .c files in test and run them together to check whether sleep works correctly.

With this setup, sleep2 should run ten times before sleep1 runs once.

At this point, the assignment is complete. Most of the content above was based on the two blogs mentioned earlier. I spent a lot of time understanding their code and tracing the existing code before trying to write it myself. This is just a record for myself; I still need to spend more time developing a deeper understanding of the system architecture before I can work with it more comfortably. I also tried the optimization mentioned in Nini’s blog for checking which threads should wake up. I will add it later if I have time. Well.
